USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture without further escalation or rollback. Let the existing $34B in tariffs (List 1) and the imminent $16B (List 2) work through the system while the $200B List 3 comment period plays out. Use this window to signal willingness to negotiate if China offers structural concessions on IP and tech transfer, but do not initiate talks from a position of weakness.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of -0.3 reflects a moderate opportunity rather than a threat. The US economy is performing strongly — industrial production at 103.4 (up 1.6% over the period), unemployment near record lows, and consumer sentiment still elevated at 97.9 despite a mild decline from 101.4 in March (country_health: UMCSENT). The Fed is tightening (1.42% → 1.91%), the dollar has strengthened 5.4% (DTWEXBGS: 107.1 → 112.9), and there is no evidence of broad macro damage from the tariffs so far.

The structural asymmetry favors the US: China exports ~$500B to the US vs. ~$130B US exports to China, meaning China runs out of tariff headroom first. China's retaliatory $34B (timeline: 2018-07-06) targeted agriculture strategically — soybean prices have fallen ~20% since April (CNBC, July 24), and farm incomes in key Trump states are under real pressure. However, the administration has announced a $12B emergency farmer aid package (CNBC, July 24), and the political damage is containable given the strength of the broader economy.

Key risk factors cut both ways. On the opportunity side: the ZTE denial order was lifted on July 13 after a $1B fine + $400M escrow (Federal Register, July 23), demonstrating the US can deploy devastating non-tariff leverage and then extract concessions — a template for broader negotiations. On the risk side: the $200B List 3 (proposed July 10) would significantly broaden the tariff scope to consumer goods, potentially raising prices for US consumers and drawing in more political opposition. The bipartisan criticism of the ZTE deal (NYT, July 13; The Verge, July 13) shows domestic political constraints on the administration's China policy.

The action score of +0.1 (hold) reflects that the US is already in a strong escalatory posture — $34B active, $16B imminent, $200B in the pipeline, with matching Chinese retaliation already absorbed. Further unilateral escalation now risks: (a) accelerating the tariff spiral into consumer goods territory with real domestic price effects, (b) further alienating allies (EU, Mexico, Canada have already imposed $22B in retaliatory tariffs per Politico, July 6), and (c) giving China a rallying narrative of American aggression. The smarter play is to hold pressure, let China's export sector feel the squeeze, and wait for Beijing to signal willingness to discuss structural reforms. If China makes a genuine offer on IP protection and tech transfer, that is the moment to negotiate — not before.
key_factors: US economy strong — industrial production rising, consumer sentiment near 100, unemployment low
Asymmetric trade flows favor US: China runs out of tariff retaliation room first
Agricultural sector under real pressure — soybean prices down 20%, farm aid package announced
ZTE denial order lifted July 13 after $1.4B settlement — demonstrates non-tariff leverage
List 3 ($200B) in comment period — escalation to consumer goods carries domestic risk
No active negotiations since May truce collapsed (May 29)
Allies (EU, Mexico, Canada) imposing retaliatory tariffs — multi-front trade conflict

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines).
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
Consumer sentiment: 101.4 (Mar) → 97.9 (Jul). Still elevated but declining.
Broad dollar index: 107.1 (Jan) → 112.9 (Jul). Strong dollar environment.
Fed funds rate: 1.42% (Feb) → 1.91% (Jul). Tightening cycle underway.
Soybean prices have plunged nearly 20 percent since April when China first announced the 25 percent tariff on U.S. soybeans.
Order Terminating Denial Order against ZTE. ZTE paid $1B fine and $400M escrow.
China's retaliatory tariffs on $34 billion worth of U.S. goods are directly aimed at rural regions of the country that voted heavily for President Donald Trump.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should signal willingness to negotiate while maintaining current retaliatory posture. Do not escalate further — the $200B List 3 is already proposed and additional provocation would trigger it. Use the yuan's 7% depreciation since mid-April as a quiet offset to tariff damage. Engage diplomatically through multiple channels to de-escalate before the situation reaches $500B coverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.5 reflects that US tariffs have moved from rhetoric to reality — $34B List 1 is in force (July 6), List 3 ($200B) is proposed (July 10), and Trump has threatened all $500B of Chinese exports. The ZTE denial order (April 16) demonstrated devastating non-tariff leverage: a single Commerce Department action nearly shut down a major Chinese firm, exposing China's dependence on US semiconductor supply chains. China's yuan has depreciated ~7% against the dollar since mid-April, which partially offsets tariff costs but raises capital flight risks reminiscent of the destabilizing 2015 devaluation. J.P. Morgan analysts (July 18) warned the trade war hit during China's critical deleveraging phase, creating a policy bind between tightening for financial stability and loosening for growth. China's retaliatory tariffs on US agriculture (soybeans, pork) target politically sensitive US regions, providing leverage, but China cannot match tariffs dollar-for-dollar given the trade asymmetry ($500B exports vs. $130B imports). The action_score of -0.15 (negotiate) reflects that China has already retaliated in kind and further escalation risks triggering List 3 before its economic damage can be absorbed. The smarter play is to let the yuan depreciation work quietly, engage diplomatically, and avoid giving the US justification for the $200B escalation while the domestic economy absorbs the initial shock.
key_factors: US List 1 ($34B) tariffs in force since July 6 with matching Chinese retaliation
US List 3 ($200B) proposed July 10 — imminent threat of further escalation
ZTE denial order (April) demonstrated devastating non-tariff tech leverage
Yuan depreciated ~7% vs dollar since mid-April — partial offset but capital flight risk
Trade asymmetry limits China's ability to match tariffs dollar-for-dollar
Trade war hit during critical deleveraging phase — policy bind between tightening and growth support
China's agricultural retaliation targets US politically sensitive regions but has limits

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines).
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.

J.P. Morgan: 'The trade war is complicating China's efforts to fix its economy... the timing couldn't have been worse. After years of handwringing, China finally began to focus in earnest on curbing credit growth — its Achilles's heel — from around mid-2017.'

China's currency fell to a near 11-month low. Since June 14, it has lost about 4 percent. Strategists said China has not intentionally driven down the yuan, but it is not taking actions it often takes to stabilize it.
The value of China's renminbi has fallen over 7 percent against the dollar since mid-April. A lower renminbi makes China's exports cheaper to foreign buyers.
